Senator McKim [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2022-02-10.172.3): > *This amendment would prevent listed companies from holding wholly virtual AGMs. It's been revised to align it with the amendments agreed to in the House to establish a review into these provisions of the bill. By their nature, listed companies have a public responsibility and the parliament should ensure that their AGMs are conducted in a publicly observable manner. Allowing listed companies to hold hybrid AGMs will provide an opportunity for all of the issues associated with virtual meetings to be sorted out and for there to be a real-world confirmation of their purported benefits. Until then, wholly virtual AGMs for listed companies should not be allowed and shareholders should retain the opportunity to sit in the same room as the executive and the board to bear witness to exactly what they are up to and have the capacity to hold them to account for their actions.* ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd037), the bill was introduced in order to: > * *allow companies to use technology to execute company documents such as contracts and deeds and to also sign meetings-related documents and provide those to their members and* > * *allow companies and registered schemes to hold hybrid meetings (which give members the option of either attending in person or remotely).*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2022-02-10.181.1) to pass the bill in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). Because the bill has already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd037), the bill was introduced in order to: > * *allow companies to use technology to execute company documents such as contracts and deeds and to also sign meetings-related documents and provide those to their members and* > * *allow companies and registered schemes to hold hybrid meetings (which give members the option of either attending in person or remotely).*

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 permanently allows companies, registered schemes and their officers to use digital technologies for meetings, sending materials and executing documents, replacing temporary COVID-19 relief expiring 31 March 2022. It requires companies to give shareholders a reasonable opportunity to participate, including speaking or asking questions orally and in writing, and allows shareholders with at least 5% voting power to request an independent report on a poll.

The speaker supported making virtual annual general meetings permanent but moved an amendment for an independent review within two years, focusing on whether small shareholders can still hold directors to account.

The speaker supported the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, arguing its two core elements—expanding electronic document signing and allowing virtual or hybrid annual general meetings—will increase efficiency, transparency, and shareholder access, particularly for smaller investors who previously could not attend physical meetings.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, which enables virtual and hybrid AGMs, should balance accessibility benefits against the reduced scrutiny and engagement of shareholders, noting the Australian Shareholders Association's criticism that virtual meetings lack dynamism and accountability compared to in-person formats. The speech also paid tribute to historian Stuart Macintyre, citing his works like *The History Wars* and *Australia's Boldest Experiment*.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 should make permanent the temporary relief allowing companies to hold meetings electronically and execute documents digitally, citing positive pandemic experiences and increased shareholder participation.

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 would increase flexibility for listed companies and shareholder-board interactions, with Labor’s opposition unsurprising given their history.

The speaker argued in support of the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, which makes permanent temporary COVID-19 relief allowing companies to hold hybrid meetings and use electronic signatures, reducing regulatory burden and saving an estimated $430 million per year for 10 years.

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 permanently allows companies to hold physical, hybrid, or virtual meetings (if permitted by their constitution), receive documents electronically or in hard copy, and execute documents using electronic or wet-ink signatures, with a 12-month opt-in review of annual general meetings.

This means that they voted to agree with the main idea of the bill and will now discuss it in greater detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd023), the purpose of the bill is to: > * *establish a new remote engagement program payment to be paid to job seekers who participate in a remote engagement placement and* > * *remove provisions that establish or refer to the now non-operational Community Development Employment Projects (CDEP) Scheme and related CDEP Scheme Participant Supplement.*

The government introduced the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021 to create a new supplementary payment of $100–$190 per fortnight for jobseekers in remote pilot communities who volunteer for 15–18 hours per week in work-like placements, aiming to co-design a replacement for the Community Development Program (CDP) by 2023. The bill also repeals obsolete provisions from the former Community Development Employment Projects (CDEP) Scheme.

The bill delays long-overdue changes to the failed Community Development Program, fails to address housing and essential services in remote Australia, and should be replaced with Labor's policy of a remote employment program offering real jobs, proper wages, and community control.

The speaker argued that the Coalition government's Community Development Program (CDP) and its replacement, the Regional Engagement Program (REP), have failed remote Indigenous communities, increasing poverty and stunting job creation. They committed a future Labor government to replacing these with a program supporting sustainable, community-controlled employment, and noted that one in three children in the Northern Territory live in poverty under the current government.

The speaker argued that the government misled Parliament about Medicare privatisation plans, citing a 2016 statement by Malcolm Turnbull, and that the Remote Engagement Program bill fails to address key flaws of the Community Development Program. Labor will support the bill for its $5,200 supplementary payment over two years to 200 trial participants, but stated it does not create real jobs or adequately support remote and Indigenous communities.

The speaker argued that the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021 addresses the lack of employment opportunities in remote Australia, citing research that work improves health, wellbeing, and reduces poverty and social exclusion. They noted that less than two per cent of actively trading businesses are located in remote areas, which disproportionately affects Indigenous Australians.

Introduced the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021, which creates a pilot program for a new supplementary payment to eligible jobseekers in remote communities who volunteer for at least 15 hours per week in skill-building placements, aiming to address the decline in Indigenous employment from 54% to 49% between 2007-08 and 2018-19. The pilot will replace the Community Development Program (CDP) in 2023 and is part of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap.

The speaker argued that the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021 fails to create real, long-term jobs and continues the failed Community Development Program, which pays below minimum wage ($11.20 per hour), penalises participants at 25 times the rate of urban jobactive, and costs $360 million per year for only 2,682 jobs with 26-week outcomes—an amount that could directly employ 19,700 people. The speaker called for scrapping the CDP and replacing it with a program offering proper wages and real jobs, and criticised the government's co-design approach and expansion of cashless debit cards.

The speaker supported the Remote Engagement Program Bill 2021, which creates a supplementary payment for jobseekers in remote pilot sites such as the Ngaanyatjarra lands, and opposed Labor's bill to scrap the cashless debit card trial, arguing it would end the Job Ready Pilot Program in Goldfields shires like Laverton, Leonora, Menzies and Coolgardie.

The speaker supported the bill and amendment, arguing that the government's Community Development Program (CDP) has failed and should be replaced with a locally controlled employment program that provides award wages, superannuation, and entitlements, similar to the old Community Development Employment Program (CDEP) which was abolished by the Howard government.

The bill establishes a pilot program for remote employment services, creating a new supplementary payment for eligible jobseekers to participate in work-like placements that build skills and benefit their communities, ahead of replacing the Community Development Program in 2023.

The Social Security Legislation Amendment (Remote Engagement Program) Bill 2021 enables a new payment for a co-designed remote employment program, replacing the Community Development Program (CDP) in 2023 as part of the Morrison government's reform to support economic recovery and close the gap for Indigenous Australians. The program sunsets in 2023.

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 lowers the registration threshold for political campaigners from $500,000 to $100,000 in electoral expenditure, and introduces a new requirement to register if spending at least $14,500 and one-third of revenue. The bill implements recommendation 18 of the JSCEM report on the 2019 federal election to align transparency rules for political actors with those for parties and candidates.

Labor opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021, arguing it would lower the political campaigner threshold for charities and not-for-profits from $500,000 or two-thirds of annual income to $100,000 or one-third, imposing heavy disclosure requirements and foreign-donation bans that silence critics. The speaker moved a second reading amendment calling for the donation disclosure threshold to be reduced from $14,500 to a fixed $1,000 with real-time disclosure, and criticised the Morrison government for failing to deliver a national anti-corruption commission and for pursuing voter ID laws.

The speaker argued the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would enhance transparency by requiring organisations spending over $100,000 or $14,500 (if over a third of annual revenue) on electoral expenditure to register as political campaigners, implementing recommendation 18 of the 2019 election inquiry. The speaker also detailed personal experiences of abuse during the 2019 campaign in the marginal seat of Robertson, including a verbal tirade at Woy Woy pre-poll, and condemned such behaviour as undemocratic.

The bill extends donation disclosure requirements to all political campaigners, not just political parties, to reduce foreign interference and increase transparency in electoral funding. The reforms follow the 2019 election inquiry which heard about intimidation of candidates, including the member for Boothby.

The speaker supported the bill's original provisions lowering the registration threshold for political campaigners from $500,000 to $100,000, but opposed the government's last-minute addition of 35 new provisions without consultation, moving an amendment to postpone the vote and calling for a lower disclosure threshold of $1,000.

The bill reduces thresholds for registering as a political campaigner, imposing retrospective compliance costs on charities and small community groups, while the speaker argued it is a cynical attempt to protect the major-party duopoly rather than genuinely increase transparency.

The speaker argued that the government's Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would silence charities and stifle democracy, contrasting it with Labor's proposed real-time disclosure of political donations with a $1,000 threshold. They noted the 'Hands Off Our Charities' coalition of 100 leading charities, including Anglicare Australia, Amnesty International, and the Australian Conservation Foundation, opposes the bill.

The bill lowers the threshold for registering as a political campaigner from $500,000 to $100,000 or one-third of annual income, which would burden small local advocacy groups like Save Willow Grove, Parramatta Park campaigners, and Westmead Push for Palliative Care with excessive red tape, while failing to address the need for broader transparency reforms through proper consultation.

The speaker argued that the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 targets smaller charities, environmental groups, and unions—such as the Australian Conservation Foundation, Bob Brown Foundation, WWF, RSPCA, St Vincent de Paul, and several unions—to silence dissent and protect the government, rather than improving transparency or democracy.

The speaker thanked committee members and commended the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 to the House, arguing it strengthens election integrity by extending funding disclosure requirements to political actors and modernising the Commonwealth Electoral Act to protect voters from being misled.

The speaker argued that the government's 35 last-minute amendments to the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would restrict freedom of speech and apply retrospectively, targeting charities and welfare groups while ignoring billionaires like Clive Palmer who buy elections. They opposed the amendments, calling the process a strategy to silence critics and pander to the far right, and demanded caps on corporate and billionaire donations instead.

The speaker opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Voter Integrity) Bill 2021, arguing it is a voter suppression tool that would require all electors to prove identity despite vanishingly low rates of multiple voting (0.001% of 16 million voters, with only 24 referred for investigation). The speaker also criticised the government for failing to establish a national integrity commission and for allowing government members to spread COVID-19 misinformation.

The independent member for Warringah criticised a deal between major parties that bargained one piece of legislation for another, opposing government amendments to the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 that would retroactively impose new reporting obligations and administrative burdens on non-profit organisations for their 2019 election advocacy.
The bill would change the military discipline system for the Australian Defence Force.
It would expand the disciplinary infringement scheme for minor breaches, remove one level of summary authority, and create new service offences.
The new offences include failure to perform duty, cyber-bullying, and failure to notify a change in circumstances affecting a benefit or allowance.
Expands the disciplinary infringement scheme to deal with minor breaches of military discipline more effectively.
Removes the subordinate summary authority to simplify the enforcement of minor disciplinary issues.
Introduces new service offences for failure to perform duty, cyber-bullying, and failure to notify a change in circumstances.
Members of the Australian Defence Force and those administering military discipline.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was introduced to reform the military discipline system, including expanding the disciplinary infringement scheme with a new senior discipline officer role, removing the subordinate summary authority, and adding new service offences for cyberbullying, receipt of a benefit or allowance, and failure to perform a duty.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 introduces a three-tier disciplinary system to streamline minor breaches via infringement notices, reduce delays, and improve mental health outcomes for ADF personnel, while also addressing cyberbullying as a new offence.

The speaker cautiously welcomed the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, which expands the disciplinary infringement scheme and introduces new offences including cyberbullying, but criticised insufficient consultation and announced Labor would refer the bill to a Senate committee inquiry, reserving final position until the inquiry reports.

The speaker expressed condolences for two soldiers who died near Townsville and supported the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, arguing it would streamline handling of minor disciplinary matters while preserving members' rights. They also criticised the Prime Minister for using the Australian national flag as a face mask during COVID and backed referring the bill to a Senate committee for scrutiny by 14 October.

The speaker argued that the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 will provide commanders with better tools to manage disciplinary matters efficiently and fairly, introducing new service offences such as cyberbullying to maintain morale and operational capability in the ADF.

The speaker supported the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, arguing it modernises the military justice system by introducing cyberbullying as a specific offence and improving efficiency for lower-level disciplinary processes. The speaker also paid tribute to ADF personnel involved in the Afghanistan withdrawal and the 41 fallen Australian service members.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was argued to be necessary for modernising military discipline, enabling faster resolution of workplace issues and adapting to changing societal expectations and technology.

The speaker acknowledged the 70th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty and referenced recent events at Hamid Karzai International Airport while addressing the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021.

The speaker acknowledged the 70th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty and the loss of 13 US personnel at Hamid Karzai International Airport to ISIS-K, and expressed support for the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, which aims to simplify the military discipline system, reduce delays, and empower commanders to address poor behaviour quickly.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was commended to the House, reforming military discipline under the Defence Force Discipline Act 1982 by allowing minor breaches to be managed as disciplinary infringements and introducing a new cyberbullying service offence for the Australian Defence Force.

The Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 was moved to establish a governance board for the APVMA, streamline chemical reporting processes, and introduce incentives for including priority uses on product labels. The bill creates a part-time board with a chair, CEO, and three members, extends data protection periods up to five years for certain uses, and broadens the APVMA's enforcement powers.

The speaker criticised the government for moving the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority from Canberra to Armidale, arguing it was politically motivated and caused staff losses, and noted the government later breached its own policy order by allowing up to 50 staff to work in Canberra. The opposition supported the bill's efficiency measures but condemned the government's repeated delays on agricultural legislation.

The speaker supported the bill to establish a governance board for the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority, improving oversight of chemicals like glyphosate, and noted agriculture employs 329,000 Australians, with a goal of becoming a $100 billion industry by 2030.

The speaker argued that the relocation of the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) from Canberra to Armidale was a destructive, anti-science move that cost hundreds of millions of dollars, caused the loss of half its scientific staff, and created major delays. The bill establishes a governance board costing $400,000–$600,000 annually, which industry groups oppose, and the speaker criticised the government for lacking transparency and prioritising votes over science.

The Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 establishes a five-person skills-based governance board for the APVMA, ceases the advisory board, and introduces measures to streamline processes, enable computerised decision-making, strengthen sanctions for misleading information, and improve voluntary recall transparency.
